# Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta (SN 8)
**ID:** SN 8
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn8

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta* (SN 8) is the eighth section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Sagāthavagga* [Bodhi 2003; von Hinüber 1996]. It comprises 12 discourses (SN 8.1–8.12) framed around verses spoken by the venerable Vaṅgīsa, whom the Buddha declared the foremost of his disciples gifted with inspirational, impromptu speech (*paṭibhānavantānaṁ*, AN I 24) [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. Renowned for his literary sophistication and spontaneous verse compositions, Vaṅgīsa's poems candidly portray his early struggles as a newly ordained monk fighting sexual attraction and discontent (*arati*), as well as his joyful devotion praising the Buddha and senior disciples such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and Aññā Koṇḍañña [Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994; SuttaCentral].
Within Pali literature, the verses of the *Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta* closely correspond to the 71 verses constituting the *Vaṅgīsattheragāthā* (Thag 1209–1279), the longest chapter in the *Theragāthā*, though the *Theragāthā* recension lacks the prose narrative settings found in the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003; von Hinüber 1996]. Text-reuse analysis confirms substantial overlap between SN 8 and both Thag 21.1 and the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. In addition, the fifth discourse (*Subhāsitasutta*, SN 8.5) shares nearly its entire text with the *Subhāsita Sutta* of the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 3.3) [DharmaNexus].
All 12 suttas in the collection have parallels preserved in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* collections (T 99 and T 100), which also feature a dedicated *Vaṅgīsa* section [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. The seventh discourse (*Pavāraṇāsutta*, SN 8.7)—which celebrates the formal end of the rains retreat and presents the Buddha as a skilled physician who destroys the dart of craving [Buddhist Philosophy and Meditation Practice 2012]—possesses especially extensive cross-canonical parallels. These include versions in the Chinese *Madhyamāgama* (MĀ 121), *Ekottarikāgama* (EĀ 32.5), three individual Chinese translations (T 61, T 62, and T 63), and the Sanskrit *Pravāraṇasūtra* [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Notably, the *Madhyamāgama* parallel contains an expanded preamble describing the Buddha as the unsurpassed "Medicine-King" [Radich 2007]. Further parallels and shared stanzas exist across the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* traditions [DharmaNexus].
